title: Shortest All-Ones Multiple
statement:
Numbers written only with the digit 1, like 1, 11, 111, are called all-ones numbers. Given a positive integer k, find the shortest all-ones number that is divisible by k and return how many digits it has.

If no all-ones number is divisible by k, return -1. The number itself can be far too long for any integer type, which is why only its length is asked for.

examples.why: A multiple of 15 must end in 0 or 5, and all-ones numbers end in 1.
11111 = 41 × 271. The length is not tied to the size of k: 41 needs only 5 digits, while 7 needs 6.

hints: You cannot build the number itself. But divisibility only depends on the remainder. How does the remainder change when you append one more 1?
If the current number leaves remainder rem, the next one leaves (rem · 10 + 1) mod k. Stop when it hits 0.
There are only k possible remainders. If none of the first k lengths gives 0, a remainder has repeated and the sequence cycles forever, so return −1. Multiples of 2 or 5 can be rejected at once.

explain.intuition:
The all-ones number of length L + 1 is the one of length L times 10 plus 1. Remainders follow the same rule: rem' = (rem · 10 + 1) mod k. So you can walk through lengths 1, 2, 3, … while carrying only a number smaller than k.

When do you stop if the answer is −1? The remainder can take only k values. After k steps without a zero, some remainder must have appeared twice, and since each step depends only on the previous remainder, the sequence is stuck in a loop that never reaches 0. That pigeonhole argument caps the loop at k iterations.
steps: If k is divisible by 2 or 5, return -1 (all-ones numbers are odd and end in 1).
For len from 1 to k: set rem = (rem · 10 + 1) % k; if rem === 0, return len.
pitfalls: Building the number as an integer. Even 64-bit integers overflow after 19 digits, and k = 17 already needs 16 ones; larger k need thousands.
Looping forever when no answer exists. Without the k-step bound the loop never ends for k = 2.
Assuming the answer is at most the number of digits of k. k = 81 needs 81 ones.

solutions.title: Build the number with big integers
solutions.idea: Grow the all-ones number as an arbitrary-precision integer and test divisibility, up to k digits.

solutions.title: Track only the remainder
solutions.idea: Append a 1 to the remainder instead of the number. After k steps without hitting 0, the remainders must be cycling.

followups: Return the shortest number made only of the digits 0 and 1 that k divides. What search does that become?
Prove that when k is coprime with 10, an answer always exists.
